summary: Fourth-order light first shown December 10, 1856 on a tidal islet at Crescent City. A federal light until 1965, now a museum with volunteer keepers and a private aid to navigation.

access.note: Tidal island reached on foot only at low tide; guided tours run tide permitting. Volunteer keepers live on the island.

facts.agency: Del Norte County Historical Society (operates the museum); Del Norte County (owner)

events.note: Congress appropriates $15,000 for a Crescent City light: March 3, 1855 per the NRHP nomination; May 1855 per LighthouseFriends
Dwelling and tower built to Light House Service specifications; construction begun 1856
Lit December 10, 1856
Original fourth-order Fresnel lens
Theophilus Magruder, first official keeper, per the register; LighthouseFriends says he arrived about fifteen days after the first lighting
John H. Jeffrey becomes keeper; he serves until 1914
Lighthouse Board calls the station dilapidated and recommends discontinuing it once a first-order light stands at Point St. George (as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
A wave strikes the wooden lean-to kitchen; the chimney falls and the stove sets a fire, put out by a second wave (LighthouseFriends account)
Dwelling painted light buff and tower white
Mineral oil lamps replace lard oil lamps
Whole lighthouse painted white
New fourth-order lamps installed
Lighthouse Board lists the light as fourth order, fixed white, varied by a white flash every ninety seconds
Three water tanks
Oil house
New four-panel fourth-order lens fixture, May 1907
From a white flash every ninety seconds to a white flash every fifteen seconds
Coast Guard takes over the lighthouse from the Lighthouse Service, July 1939 per the NRHP nomination; the Historical Society's page dates the takeover to 1936
Automatic light installed July 1953; LighthouseFriends says a modern 375 mm lens replaced the fourth-order lens; the Historical Society's page says a fifth-order Drumm lens was kept until 1965
Lighthouse leased to Del Norte County, November 1, 1953
Tsunami from the Alaska earthquake reaches Crescent City about midnight March 27-28; the lighthouse is not damaged
Federal light discontinued; a light at the end of the new harbor jetty replaces it
Federal government transfers the property to the county for historical monument purposes
State Historical Landmark No. 951, October 4, 1982
Becomes a private aid to navigation, December 10, 1982, with a 1,000-watt beacon

corrections.proposed: Del Norte County Historical Society (operates the museum); Del Norte County (owner)
corrections.why: The current value is garbled and describes the aid's status, not who operates or owns the station. The NRHP nomination names Del Norte County as owner, and the Historical Society runs the museum.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The federal light was discontinued about 1965 and relit as a private aid to navigation on December 10, 1982. Sources that describe it as lit are describing the 1982 reactivation; it is not a continuous federal light.

The historic characteristic is documented: a flash every ninety seconds in 1899 and every fifteen seconds after the May 1907 lens. The present characteristic is not established by any source read for this story (see notes_for_editor).

notes_for_editor: 1) Present characteristic not established: the record's Fl W 30s appears in Wikipedia's infobox only (lead, not cited); the story gives the 1899 and 1907 characteristics. Check the USCG Light List. 2) Lens conflict: the record says order 5 in place; the NRHP and LighthouseFriends give a fourth-order original lens; the Historical Society page says a fifth-order Drumm lens was kept until 1965; LighthouseFriends says a 375 mm modern lens replaced the fourth-order lens in 1953. Current lens and its location unresolved, so lens status is 'unknown'. 3) Focal height: NRHP gives 77 ft above mean high water (23.5 m, used in facts); Coons gives 74 ft above mean sea level; the record has 23.0 m. Range: the record gives 14 nm; Coons says '14 miles' with no unit; Wikipedia says 12 nm (not cited). 4) NRHP latitude is printed as 40 degrees 44 minutes; this is almost certainly 41 degrees (the record's OSM position, 41.744, and Wikipedia's 41 degrees 44 minutes 39 seconds agree). 5) Coast Guard takeover: 1936 (Historical Society) vs July 1939 (NRHP). Not resolved. 6) Dunbar 1933-1936: the register lists him as principal keeper; LighthouseFriends says a lamplighter served in those years. Recorded as head keeper with a note. 7) Magruder: register starts 1857; LighthouseFriends says he arrived about fifteen days after the first lighting in December 1856. 8) The record's 1983 nrhp_listed date is unverified: the nomination form is dated April 1982 and the state landmark October 4, 1982; no source read gives the 1983 listing. 9) The 1855 appropriation: March 3 (NRHP) vs May (LighthouseFriends). 10) The 1879 wave and kitchen fire, and the undated rogue wave, come only from LighthouseFriends, which is a secondary compilation; no primary record was found. 11) Peggy and Clarence Coons are named only as curators in their published account; no personal details beyond that account are used. 12) The 1880 Sacramento newspaper item was the only useful Chronicling America hit; searches for keeper names returned unrelated pages. 13) The 1897 and 1899 Lighthouse Board volumes are cited by scan page; printed page numbers were not read, so cite by scan page. 14) LighthouseFriends is an all-rights-reserved site: facts are paraphrased and only one short phrase is quoted. 15) The keeper register spelling 'Henessey' is as printed by the archive; variants unchecked. 16) Fact-check 2026-10-22: the NRHP says the central tower is 77 feet above mean high water and contained a fourth-order lens; focal_height_m 23.5 uses that figure as the lens height, and Coons gives the lighthouse as 74 feet above mean sea level. The mainland-reservation passage (scan 440) is in the report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1897, not 1896-1897. The 1899 list entry (scan 47) is in the report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1899. The NRHP names the dwelling as stone and does not say the tower's material; LighthouseFriends calls the tower brick, and the story says so.
